posts.title: The Three-Anchor Baseline Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: One latest version is rarely enough for automated publishing. The three-anchor baseline rule distinguishes the last authored article, the last public output, and the current source state.

posts.title: The Draft-Only Source-Advance Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Draft creation changes the authoring baseline, not necessarily the public site. The draft-only source-advance rule preserves both facts without treating an unpublished placeholder as a release.

posts.title: The Remote-Draft-Tail Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Clean is not current. The remote-draft-tail rule requires an authoring run to absorb or account for newly created drafts before it produces the next publication.

posts.title: The Scheduled-Window Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Schedules describe intent, not an exact execution guarantee. The scheduled-window rule uses measured delivery windows and explicit escalation thresholds for reliable publishing automation.

posts.title: The Branch-Name Catch-Up Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: The branch-name catch-up rule separates published content from local reference hygiene. After a successful side-path release, update the durable working baseline so future automation starts from the truth.

posts.title: The Rejoin-Before-Rebind Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: An isolated copy is not automatically orphaned work. The rejoin-before-rebind rule checks for already-integrated content before creating duplicate recovery branches or releases.

posts.title: The Semantic-No-Op Advance Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A new version is not always a new story. The semantic-no-op advance rule updates operational baselines while reserving editorial announcements for reader-visible change.

posts.title: The Merge-Base Deletion Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: An absent page is not automatically a deletion. The merge-base deletion rule asks whether a source actually removed content or merely lacks a change introduced elsewhere.

posts.title: The Publish-Surface Novelty Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Not every repository change is a publishing change. The publish-surface novelty rule separates reader-visible updates from operational churn so automation does not manufacture a false content backlog.

posts.title: The Same-Tree Dedup Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A new event is not necessarily new content. The same-tree dedup rule groups equivalent candidates before ranking or publishing them, reducing duplicate releases and noisy review.

posts.title: The Authority-Scoped Convergence Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: There is no such thing as globally converged publishing state. The authority-scoped convergence rule requires every claim of alignment to name the source that grants release permission.

posts.title: The One-Step Catch-Up Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Progress is not convergence. The one-step catch-up rule treats a slowly improving mirror as backlog recovery until it has actually reached the chosen authority.

posts.title: The Snapshot-Anchor Lag Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Freshness has two dimensions: when a snapshot was made and what editorial state it inherited. The snapshot-anchor lag rule keeps a new timestamp from overruling an older source baseline.

posts.title: The Refreshed-Remote Role Check for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: A reachable remote tip is not automatically the right publish candidate. Candidate election should classify branch role and content type before following a freshly fetched head.

posts.title: The Lineage-Over-Timestamp Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: When a later unbranched snapshot forks from an older commit and drops newer published posts, publish selection must prefer authoritative lineage over raw recency.

posts.title: The Snapshot-Stream Identity Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Repeated worktree snapshot commits with the same generator pattern should be tracked as a named side stream outside the publish branch. That preserves evidence and keeps backlog, freshness, and reconciliation logic attached to the authoritative lineage.

posts.title: The Snapshot-Commit Quarantine Rule for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Autonomous publishing should not count every local content-bearing commit as release backlog. Snapshot commits on side refs need their own quarantined state until they land on the elected publishing lineage.
